No matter the size of the books, there was none he did not like.
Although he did not enjoy the art of war,
he still read it.
Although he read books on deities and immortality,
he suppressed and did not believe them,
considering them to be false and exaggerated.
At this time, after Emperor Líng died,
the world was in turmoil.
Only Jiāozhōu was relatively peaceful.
Many unusual people from the north came and stayed there,
many practicing techniques for becoming deities, abstaining from grains, and achieving longevity.
At that time, many people studied these techniques.
Mùzǐ often challenged them with the Five Classics.
The Daoist practitioners and magicians dared not respond.
This was comparable to Mèng Kē refuting Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí.
Before this, Mùzǐ had taken his mother to Jiāozhǐ to avoid the world.
At the age of twenty-six, he returned to Cāngwú to marry.
The governor, hearing of his devotion to learning,
paid a visit and requested him to be appointed as an official.
At that time, he was in his prime,
with his heart set on learning.
Moreover, seeing the world in chaos,
he had no intention of serving.
In the end, he did not accept the position.
At this time, the various prefectures and commanderies were suspicious of each other, cut off, and not communicating.
The Grand Administrator considered him erudite and knowledgeable.
He sent him to pay respects to Jīngzhōu.
Móu Zǐ thought that high office was easy to decline,
but a mission was difficult to refuse.
So he prepared solemnly to depart.
It happened that he was summoned by the Governor of the province as an outstanding scholar,
but he again claimed illness and did not rise to the occasion.
The Governor's younger brother was the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng.
He was killed by the General of the Household Zé Róng.
At that time, the Governor sent the Cavalry Commandant Liú Yàn,
leading troops to assist.
Fearing that outsiders would suspect them and the troops would not be able to advance,
the Governor then invited Móu Zǐ, saying:
"My younger brother was killed by a rebellious bandit.
The pain of flesh and blood stirs in my heart.
I intend to send Commandant Liú to go,
but I fear that outsiders will be suspicious, making it difficult for people to pass.
You possess both literary and military abilities and have the talent to engage in special negotiations.
Now I would like to trouble you.
How about requesting a passage through Línglíng and Guìyáng as a way to get through?"
Móu Zǐ said,
"Having been fed and kept in the stable, having been favored for a long time,
a righteous man forgets himself, determined to prove his worth."
So he prepared solemnly to depart.
It happened that his mother suddenly died, and he was unable to go after all.
After a long time, he retreated and reflected:
"Because of my eloquence, I am frequently sent on missions.
In these turbulent times, it is not the season to make oneself prominent."
Thereupon, he sighed and said.
"Lǎozǐ abandoned sagacity and discarded wisdom.
He cultivated himself and preserved his true nature.

The Son of Heaven could not make him a subject.

Therefore, he is worthy of esteem."

Simultaneously studying the five thousand words of Lǎozǐ.

道與不道如金比草。 Having the Dao and not having the Dao are like comparing gold to grass;
Goodness and fortune are like white and black squares.
How could they not be different?
So how can you say they are the same?
Someone asked:
Confucius said,
“If you cannot yet serve men, how can you serve spirits?
If you do not yet know life, how can you know death?”
This is what the sages rejected.
Now, Buddhist teachings frequently discuss matters of life and death and the affairs of ghosts and spirits.
This is hardly the language of sages and wise men.
Those who tread the path
should be empty and without desire, returning to simplicity and genuineness.
Why then discuss life and death to disturb their will, and speak of ghosts and spirits as trivial matters?
Móu Zǐ said:
If that is what you say,
you are someone who sees the external but doesn't recognize the internal.
Confucius disliked Zǐ Lù's not asking about the fundamental and the derivative, and used this to restrain him.
The Classic of Filial Piety says:
“Build ancestral temples to allow the spirits to enjoy offerings.”
"In the Spring and Autumn period, sacrifices were made at the appropriate times to remember them."
It also says:
"In life, serve them with love and respect;
in death, serve them with grief and sorrow."
Does this not teach people to serve ghosts and spirits and to know about life and death?
The Duke of Zhōu prayed for King Wǔ, saying,
"Dàn is multi-talented and skilled, capable of serving ghosts and spirits."
What was that all about?
Are not the realms of life and death discussed in the Buddhist scriptures
of the same kind?
Lǎozǐ said,
"Know his son, then return and keep to his mother,
and to the end of your days you will suffer no harm."
He also said,
"Use its light, return to its brightness."
He leaves no calamity to himself."
This Way is where life and death tend towards,
Where good fortune and misfortune dwell.
The essence of the ultimate Way truly values tranquility.
Is it that the Buddhist school likes to speak?
It is only that one must answer when asked.
Do bells and drums ring by themselves?
They only make a sound when struck.
Someone asked:
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Yí and Dí barbarians, even if they have rulers,
Are not as good as the various Xià states without them."
Mèngzǐ criticized Chén Xiāng,
Who changed to learn the methods of Xǔ Xíng, saying:
"I have heard of using Xià to transform the Yí,
But I have never heard of using the Yí to transform Xià.
You, sir, learned the Way of Yáo, Shùn, Zhōu, and Kǒng when you were young,
But now you abandon it,
And instead learn the methods of the Yí and Dí barbarians.
Are you not utterly confused?"
Móuzǐ said:
"These are merely residual words from when I had not yet understood the Great Way.
If you can be said to have seen the splendor of ritual and institutions,
yet be ignorant of the substance of morality and virtue;
glimpsed the light of a torch,
yet not beheld the sun in the celestial court.
What Kǒngzǐ 孔子 spoke of was correcting the ways of the world;
what Mèng Kē 孟軻 spoke of was detesting exclusiveness.
In the past, Kǒngzǐ 孔子 wanted to live among the Nine Yi, saying:
"If a gentleman dwells there, what baseness is there?"
And when Zhòngní 仲尼 was not tolerated in Lǔ 魯 and Wèi 衛,
and Mèng Kē 孟軻 was not employed in Qí 齊 and Liáng 梁,
how could they have served in the lands of the Yi and Di?
Yǔ 禹 came from the Western Qiāng 羌, yet became a sage;
Gǔsǒu 瞽叟 gave birth to Shùn 舜, yet he was obstinate and foolish;
Yóuyú 由余 was born in the Dí 狄 state, yet he hegemonized Qín 秦;
Guǎn 蔡 spread slander though they came from the Hé 河 and Luò 洛 regions.
The *Zhuan* says:
"The star of the North Star
is in the center of the heavens,
and to the north of man."
Looking at it this way,
the Han lands are not necessarily the center of heaven.
The Buddhist scriptures say
that all living things above and below, and all creatures containing blood, belong to the Buddha.
Therefore, I respect and study them.
Why should I abandon the ways of Yáo 堯, Shùn 舜, Zhōu 周, and Kǒng 孔?
Gold and jade do not harm each other;
the Suí 隨 pearl does not obstruct the Bì 碧 jade.
To call others deluded is to delude oneself.
Question:
Using one's father's wealth to beg for recognition from strangers
cannot be called benevolence.
When both parents are still alive, killing oneself to substitute for another
cannot be called righteousness.
Now, the Buddhist scriptures say
that Prince Sudāna
used his father's wealth to give to people from afar,
and gave the kingdom's precious elephant to an enemy.
He even gave his wife and children to others.
To not respect one's parents
but respect others
is called violating propriety.
To not love one's parents
but love others
is called violating virtue.
Sūdàna is neither filial nor benevolent,
yet the Buddhists venerate him.
Isn't this strange?
Móuzǐ said:
The meaning of the Five Classics is to establish the eldest legitimate son as heir.
King Tài had the intention to favor Chāng,
so he changed Jì to be the heir,
thus accomplishing the Zhou dynasty's enterprise
and achieving great peace.
According to the principle of marrying a wife, one must inform one's parents.
Shùn did not inform his parents but married to fulfill a great moral principle.
A virtuous person must be sought after with betrothal gifts,
Worthy officials await summons.
Yī Yǐn 尹尹 carried the cauldron to seek audience with Tāng 湯.
Níng Qī 甯戚 knocked on the horn to request an audience with Qí 齊.
Tāng 湯 attained kingship because of him.
Qí 齊 achieved hegemony because of him.
According to ritual, men and women do not personally hand things to each other.
But if a sister-in-law is drowning, one should offer her a hand.
This is because of the urgency of the situation.
If one sees the greater principle,
one should not be拘 (jū) bound by the small details.
How can a great man be bound by convention?
One must greatly abandon [things] to see the impermanence of the world and that wealth is not one's true treasure.
Therefore, one should freely give in charity to achieve the Great Way.
The father's country will receive its blessing.
Enemies will not be able to enter.
As for attaining Buddhahood,
parents and siblings will all be able to be delivered from the world.
Is this not being filial?
Is this not being benevolent?
Who then is truly benevolent and filial?
Someone asked:
The Buddhist path emphasizes inaction (無為; wúwéi) and joy in giving, and holding precepts with trepidation as if facing a deep abyss.
Now, Buddhist monks indulge in wine and liquor,
or keep wives and children,
buying cheap and selling dear,
engaging solely in deceitful practices.
This is the greatest hypocrisy in the world.
And the Buddhist path calls this inaction (無為; wúwéi)?
Móuzǐ said:
Craftsman Lú (Lú Shū) can give people axes, adzes, plumb lines, and ink markers,
but cannot make them skilled.
The sage can impart the Dao to people,
but cannot make them practice and follow it.
Gāoyáo could punish thieves,
but could not make greedy men into Yí Qí.
The five punishments could execute the lawless,
but could not make wicked sons into Zēng Shēn or Mǐn Zǐqiān.
Yáo could not transform Dānzhū,
and the Duke of Zhōu could not instruct Guǎncài.
Was it because the teachings of the Táng (Yáo) were not clear
or the ways of the Zhōu (Duke of Zhōu) were incomplete?
But there's nothing one can do about wicked people.
It is like worldly people mastering the Seven Classics
but being deluded by wealth and lust.
Can we then say the Six Arts are wicked and licentious?
Although the River God is divine,
he does not drown people on land.
Though the whirlwind is swift,
it cannot make settled water raise dust.
One should be concerned that people cannot practice [the Dao].
How can one say that the Buddha's path has evil in it?
Someone asked:
Confucius said,
"Extravagance leads to insubordination; frugality leads to stubbornness.
Rather than being insubordinate, I prefer stubbornness."
Shūsūn said,
Frugality is the reverence of virtue.
Extravagance is the greatest of evils.
Now, Buddhists consider emptying one's wealth for almsgiving
and viewing giving away all possessions as noble.
How can there be blessings in this?
Mù Zǐ said,
"That was one time,
this is another time."
The words of Zhòngní
detest extravagance and lack of propriety.
The criticism of Shū Sūn,
criticizing the carving of pillars by the duke,
was not forbidding almsgiving.
When Shùn farmed at Mount Lì,
his kindness did not reach the counties and villages.
When Tài Gōng slaughtered oxen,
his benevolence did not extend to his wife and children.
When they were employed,
their kindness flowed to all eight regions, and their benevolence reached the four seas.
Abundant wealth and numerous goods are valued for the ability to give, and repeated poverty is valued for the adherence to the Way.
Xǔ Yóu did not covet the four seas.
Bó Yí did not relish his state.
Yú Qīng relinquished the fief of ten thousand households
to relieve the urgency of the poor.
Each had his own aspiration.
Xī Fù Kùi, with the kindness of a pot of rice,
preserved his living space.
Xuān Mèng, because of a single meal,
To save his invaluable body.
He secretly bestows kindness unexpectedly.
The manifest reward is as bright as the white sun.
Moreover, he empties his family's wealth to generate goodwill.
His merit is as towering as Mount Sōng and Mount Tài.
As boundless as the rivers and seas.
Those who cherish goodness are answered with blessings.
Those who harbor evil are repaid with calamity.
There has never been a case of planting rice and harvesting wheat.
Or creating disaster and obtaining blessings.
Someone asked:
"Indeed, nothing surpasses sincerity in matters.
Nothing surpasses truthfulness in speech.
Lǎozǐ eliminated flowery and embellished language.
Honoring substantial and simple words.
Buddhist scriptures speak without pointing directly to the matter.
Merely broadly adopting metaphors.
Metaphors are not essential to the Dao.
Forcing disparate things into agreement is not the essence of the matter.
Although the words are abundant and the language extensive.
It is like a cart full of jade dust, not considered a treasure."
Móuzǐ said:
"Matters commonly seen by all.
Can be explained with truthfulness.
Matters seen by one person but not by another.
Are difficult to discuss with sincerity.
In the past, people who had not seen a *lín* (麒麟).
Asked those who had seen one, 'What kind of creature is a *lín*?'
One who saw it said,
"The *lín* is like a *lín*."
The questioner said,
"If I had ever seen a *lín*,
then I wouldn't be asking you.
But to say the *lín* is like a *lín*, how can this be explained?"
The one who saw it said,
"The *lín* has the body of a deer, the tail of an ox, the hooves of a deer, and the back of a horse."
The questioner gave a forced explanation.
Confucius said,
"To be not displeased when others do not understand you,
is this not the mark of a gentleman?"
*Lǎozǐ* said,
"The space between Heaven and Earth, is it not like a bellows?"
He also said,
"To compare the *Dào* to the world,
is like the streams and valleys to the rivers and seas; why adorn it with embellishments?"
The *Lúnyǔ* (Analects) says,
"To govern with virtue is like the North Star."
It uses Heaven to compare to man.
*Zǐxià* said,
"Compared to grasses and trees, they are distinguished by their differences."
The three hundred *shī* (poems)
draw on things and associate them by category.
From the various philosophers to the apocryphal texts and secret essentials of the sages,
all invariably use comparisons and draw analogies.
Why do you alone dislike the Buddha's explanation of the scriptures through comparisons and analogies?
Someone asked,
The way people conduct themselves in the world,
none do not love wealth and high status and hate poverty and lowliness,
delight in pleasure and ease and shrink from toil and weariness.
The Yellow Emperor cultivated his nature
by considering the five delicacies as supreme.
Confucius said,
"One should not tire of finely milled rice, nor of finely cut fish."
Now, the *shāmén* (沙門, monks) wear red cloth,
eat one meal a day,
shut off the six emotions,
and end their lives in this way.
What enjoyment can there be in this?
Móuzǐ (牟子) said,
"Wealth and high status are what people desire,
but if they cannot be obtained by the proper means, they should not be accepted.
Poverty and lowliness are what people hate,
but if they cannot be avoided by the proper means, they should not be rejected."
Lǎozǐ (老子) said,
"The five colors blind the eye,
the five tones deafen the ear,
the five flavors dull the palate,
racing and hunting drive the mind mad,
and rare goods lead to obstructive conduct.
The sage cares for the belly, not the eye."
How could these words be false?
Liǔxià Huì (柳下惠) would not exchange his conduct for the position of the Three Dukes.
Duàn Gānmù (段干木) would not exchange his person for the wealth of Wèi Wén (魏文).
Xǔ Yóu (許由) and Cháofù (巢父) lived in trees,
He considered himself at ease within the imperial domain.
Yí Qí starved on Shǒuyáng Mountain.
He considered himself sated with literature and martial arts.
Indeed, each simply attained his aspirations.
What dissatisfaction could there be?
Someone asked,
"If the Buddhist scriptures are profound and wonderfully ornate,
why do you not discuss them in the court,
debate them with your ruler and father,
practice them in your private quarters,
and share them with your friends?
Why then still study the classics and read the philosophers?"
Móuzǐ said,
"You have not reached the source,
yet you ask about the stream.
To display sacrificial vessels at the gates of a rampart,
to erect flags in the court,
to wear fox fur to greet a summer guest,
to wear fine linen to control the huángzhōng (lowest-pitched bell) musical instrument,
is not that they are not beautiful,
but that they are out of place and out of time.
Therefore, to hold the doctrines of Confucius
and enter the gate of Shāng Yāng,
to carry the teachings of Mèng Kē
and visit the court of Sū and Zhāng,
will yield no merit, not even an inch,
but mistakes will be a foot long.
Lǎozǐ said,
Superior scholars, upon hearing the Dao, diligently practice it.
Average scholars, upon hearing the Dao, seem to remember it, seem to forget it.
Inferior scholars, upon hearing the Dao, greatly laugh at it.
I fear such great laughter, therefore I do not discuss it.
When thirsty, one need not wait for the Jiāng Hé (Yangtze and Yellow Rivers).
Drinking well water, what would prevent one from being satiated?
Therefore, I am again studying the classics and commentaries.
Someone asked:
The land of Hàn first heard of the Buddha-Dao.
Where did it come from?
Móuzǐ said:
Formerly, Emperor Xiàomíng
dreamt of a divine person.
Whose body had sunlight and flew before the palace.
He was joyfully pleased by it.
The next day, he widely asked his ministers,
"What god is this?"
There was a knowledgeable person, Fù Yì, who said,
"I have heard that in Tiānzhú (India) there is one who has attained the Dao, called Buddha,
who flies in the empty sky
and whose body has sunlight.
It is probably that god."
Thereupon, the Emperor awoke
and sent the courtier Cài Yīn, the Imperial Guard commander Qín Jǐng, the doctoral student Wáng Zūn, and eighteen others
to the Greater Yuèzhī
to transcribe the Sutra in Forty-two Sections.
It was stored in the fourteenth room of the Stone Chamber in the Lántái.
At that time, a Buddhist temple was built outside the Yōng Gate, west of the city of Luòyáng.
On its walls were painted thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of horsemen circling a pagoda three times.
Also, at the Qingliáng Tái 清涼臺 in the southern palace,
and above the Kāiyáng 開陽 city gate, images of the Buddha were made.
During the reign of Emperor Míng, he preemptively built his mausoleum, saying,
"Xiǎnjié 顯節," and on it, images of the Buddha were also made.
At that time, the country was prosperous, the people were peaceful, and distant barbarians admired righteousness.
Scholars flourished as a result.
Someone asked:
Lǎozǐ 老子 said,
"The wise do not speak;
those who speak are not wise."
He also said,
"Great eloquence seems like stuttering;
great skill seems like clumsiness."
"The superior man is ashamed of his words exceeding his actions."
Supposing the Śramaṇas possess the ultimate Dao,
why don't they sit and practice it?
Why do they still discuss right and wrong, and argue about crookedness and straightness?
I believe this is detrimental to virtuous conduct.
Móuzǐ 牟子 said:
"Next spring there will be a great famine; if one doesn't eat this autumn..."
"The huángzhōng 黃鍾 bell responds to the cold; the guest prepares heavy furs."
"Early preparation, though early, cannot avoid being foolish."
What Lǎozǐ 老子 spoke of
refers to those who have attained the Dao.
How can those who have not attained the Dao know of it?
The Great Dao, with one word, makes the world happy.
Is this not great eloquence?
Did not Lǎozǐ say?
"To retire after accomplishing one's merit is the Way of Heaven."
Once one has retired,
what more is there to say?
Today's Śramaṇas have not yet attained the Dao,
how can they not speak?
Lǎo Shì also still speaks.
If he had nothing to say, how could he have composed the five thousand (characters)?
If one knows but does not speak, that is permissible.
But if one neither knows nor can speak, that is foolish.
Therefore, one who can speak but cannot act is a teacher of the state;
one who can act but cannot speak is a servant of the state;
one who can both act and speak is a treasure of the state.
The three kinds each have their use,
so how can they be detrimental to virtue?
Only one who can neither speak
nor act
is called a thief.
Someone asked:
According to your words,
one should only learn eloquence and cultivate rhetoric;
wouldn't that mean neglecting the cultivation of one's nature and the practice of morality?
Móu Zǐ said:
Why is it so difficult to understand?
For speech and discourse each have their proper time.
Qú Yuán said:
"When the state is governed by the Dao, be direct;
when the state is not governed by the Dao, roll up your words and keep them to yourself."
Níng Wǔzǐ was wise when the state was well-governed.
He was foolish when the state was not well-governed.
Confucius said:
To fail to speak to someone who can be spoken to is to lose a person.
To speak to someone who cannot be spoken to is to waste words.
Therefore, wisdom and foolishness each have their time.
Discussions each have their own intention.
Why would one speak and debate but not act accordingly?
Someone asked:
Why is it said that the Buddha's Way is supremely honored, supremely joyful, non-active, and tranquil?
Yet worldly people and scholars often slander and disparage it, saying
that its teachings are vague and difficult to apply,
and that its emptiness is difficult to believe?
Mú Zǐ said:
The finest flavor does not suit every palate.
The grandest sound is not comparable to ordinary ears.
When the *Xiánchí* was composed and the *Dàzhāng* was created,
when the *Xiāosháo* was played and the *Jiǔchéng* was sung,
no one harmonized with them.
But when the stringed music of Zhāng, Zhèng, and Wèi, the popular tunes of the time, were played,
people would clap their hands without needing to be asked.
Therefore, Sòng Yù said:
"When a guest sang in Yǐng,
performing a song from the Lower Village,
a thousand people joined in.
But when he played *shāng* and *jiǎo* [modes],
no one responded."
These are all people who delight in perverse sounds
One who does not understand great magnanimity.
Hán Fēi 韩非, with the view of looking through a pipe, criticized Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜.
Jiē Yú 接輿, with the distinction of fine hair, satirized Zhòng Ní 仲尼.
They were all engrossed in the small while neglecting the great.
Now, if one hears a clear *shāng* mode and calls it a *jiǎo* mode,
it is not the fault of the one plucking the strings,
but the listener's lack of discernment.
If one sees the Hé Jade 和璧 and calls it a stone,
it is not that the jade is cheap,
but that the viewer's sight is unclear.
A divine snake can sever itself and then reconnect,
but it cannot prevent others from severing it.
A spiritual tortoise can send dreams to Sòng Yuán 宋元,
but it cannot escape the net of Yùjū 豫苴.
The Great Dao is non-action; it is not seen by the common folk.
It is not ennobled by those who praise it;
it is not debased by those who slander it.
Whether it is used or not is up to Heaven.
Whether it is practiced or not depends on the time.
Whether it is believed or not is its destiny.
Someone asked:
"You, sir, use classical texts to explain Buddhist teachings.
Your words are rich and your meaning clear,
your writing is flourishing and your explanations beautiful.
Could it be that it is not your sincerity, but your eloquence, sir?"
Móuzǐ 牟子 said:
"It is not my eloquence.
It is that I have seen widely, therefore I am not perplexed."
Someone asked:
"Do you find erudition to be a skill?"
Mùzǐ said:
"It comes from the Buddhist scriptures.
Before I understood the Buddhist scriptures,
I was even more confused than you.
Though I recited the Five Classics, it was merely for show,
and never truly bore fruit.
After I saw the teachings of the Buddhist scriptures,
and examined the essentials of Lǎozǐ,
maintained a tranquil nature,
observed the practice of non-action,
and then looked back at worldly affairs,
it was like standing at the mouth of a well and peering at a stream,
or climbing Mount Sōng and Mount Dài and looking at molehills.
The Five Classics are like the five flavors,
while the Buddhist path is like the five grains.
Since I heard the Dao,
it has been like parting the clouds to see the white sun,
or bringing a torch into a dark room."
Someone asked:
"Zǐyún said, 'The classics are like rivers and seas, their writing like brocade and embroidery.'
Why don't you use the Buddhist scriptures to answer my questions,
but instead cite the Book of Poetry and the Book of Documents,
combining differences into sameness?"
Mùzǐ said:
"A thirsty person does not necessarily have to drink from the rivers and seas,
and a hungry person does not necessarily have to wait for the Óucāng granary to be full.
The Dao is established for the wise.
Argument is understood by the discerning.
Books are transmitted by those who understand.
Matters are made clear by those who see.
Because I know that you understand its meaning, I cite the matter.
To speak of the words of the Buddhist scriptures,
and discuss the essentials of inaction (wúwéi),
is like describing the five colors to a blind man,
or playing the five tones for a deaf person.
Even Shī Kuàng, though skilled, could not play a stringless zither.
Even if foxes and badgers are warm, they cannot warm a person without breath.
Gōngmíng Yí played the "Qīngjiǎo" melody for the oxen, but they continued to eat as before, not because the oxen couldn't hear, but because it didn't suit their ears.
Change it to the sound of mosquitoes and gadflies, or the bleating of a calf,
and they will wag their tails, perk up their ears, and listen eagerly. This is how poetry and books make sense to you.
Question:
Formerly, when I was in the capital,
I entered the Dōngguān and traveled through the Imperial Academy (Tàixué),
observing the standards of the outstanding scholars,
and listening to the discussions of the Confucian scholars.
I never heard that cultivating the Buddhist Dao was considered noble,
or that humbling oneself was considered superior.
Why do you indulge in it?
When one is lost, one changes the road.
When techniques are exhausted, one returns to the old ways.
Shouldn't you consider this?
Móuzǐ said:
He who is skilled at change cannot be shown deception; he who understands the Dao cannot be startled by the strange.
He who is careful with words cannot be confused by speech.
One who is versed in righteousness cannot be swayed by profit.
Lǎozi said:
"Fame is a detriment to the body;
profit is a defilement to conduct."
He also said:
"To devise deception and establish authority,
emptiness and nothingness become self-valued;
cultivating the etiquette and techniques of the boudoir, observing the occasions of contemporary customs,
rushing to seize openings and striving to conform to the current age—
these are the actions of inferior men;
they are discarded by men of middling quality.
How much more so when it comes to the boundless Great Way,
which is practiced by the highest sages?
It is as distant as the heavens,
as deep as the sea.
It is fitting that it is not compatible with those confined to peeping over walls, men of only several *rèn* high.
Indeed, it is as it should be.
They see its gate, I behold its chamber;
they gather its blossoms, I take its fruit;
they seek its completeness, I guard its oneness.
Hurry and change your path; I will tread it.
The source of misfortune and fortune,
I do not yet know what it will be like."
Someone asked:
"You use the ornate words of classics and commentaries, flowery language,
to praise Buddhist practices and extol their virtues.
In height, they surpass the pure clouds;
in breadth, they exceed the boundaries of the earth.
Is it not that you have overstepped its foundation and exaggerated its reality?
While my criticism has somewhat hit the mark and its illness.
Móu Zǐ said:
Alas! That which I praise,
is like attaching dust to Mount Sōng and Mount Tài,
or collecting morning dew and casting it into the rivers and seas.
That which you slander,
is like holding a gourd dipper and wanting to diminish the rivers and seas,
or treading on a plow and wanting to damage the Kūnlún Mountains.
Shielding the sunlight with a single palm,
or raising a clod of earth to block the rushing river.
My praise cannot make the Buddha higher,
your defamation cannot make him lower.
Someone asked:
The records of Wáng Qiáo, Chì Sōng, and the eight immortals, one hundred and seventy scrolls of divine books,
are the matters of longevity the same as the Buddhist scriptures?
Móu Zǐ said:
Comparing their categories is like the Five Hegemons compared to the Five Emperors,
Yáng Huò compared to Zhòngní.
Comparing their forms is like hillocks compared to Mount Huá and Mount Héng,
small streams compared to the rivers and seas.
Comparing their writing is like tiger skin compared to sheepskin,
coarse ramie cloth compared to brocade.
There are ninety-six kinds of Dao,
but as for being esteemed and great,
nothing surpasses the Buddhist Dao.
The books of the Immortals,
listening to them fills the ears,
Seeking to imitate them is like grasping the wind and chasing shadows.
Therefore, it is not what the great Dao takes to be right.
It is not what *wúwéi* 無為 values.
How can they be the same?
Someone asked:
"Some who practice the Dao abstain from grain and do not eat,
yet drink wine and eat meat.
They also say it is the technique of Lǎozǐ 老氏.
However, Buddhism considers wine and meat to be the highest prohibitions,
yet they eat grain instead.
How can it be so different?"
Móuzǐ 牟子 said:
